Hymenocephalus italicus is a small, bentho-pelagic grenadier that inhabits the deep continental slopes of the Mediterranean Sea, and recent collections from the central Tyrrhenian Sea have allowed a detailed examination of its life-history parameters. Morphometric analysis of a large sample of individuals indicates that the species attains a maximum total length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], a modest size that aligns with its position as one of the smaller macrourid fishes in the region. Reproductive studies focusing on gonadal maturation stages show that the total length at which 50 percent of females have initiated vitellogenesis is approximately 11 centimeters [Lp = approximately 11 centimeters], marking the transition to puberty. At this size, individuals weigh roughly 3.8 grams [Wwp = roughly 3.8 grams] wet weight, a value derived from length-weight regressions on specimens of known maturity. These data confirm that Hymenocephalus italicus matures at a relatively small body size compared to many other bathyal macrourids, a trait that may reflect the constraints of a deep-sea environment where food resources are seasonally pulsed and metabolic demands are low.

The embryonic and early larval stages of this species remain poorly documented in the wild, but comparative inference from a closely related macrourid, Coryphaenoides rupestris, provides a useful proxy for estimating initial propagule mass. Based on an assumed egg diameter of 2.6 millimeters at ovum activation, the wet weight at birth for Hymenocephalus italicus can be approximated at 0.0092 grams [Wwb = 0.0092 grams], a mass that corresponds to the yolk-sac larva stage immediately following eclosion. Newly emerged larvae are entirely endotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves until the completion of yolk-sac resorption triggers the onset of exogenous feeding. The relatively small size at hatching suggests a high fecundity but low per-offspring investment, a strategy that is common among deep-sea teleosts that produce pelagic eggs. Field records of closely related species indicate that the yolk-dependent period may last for several days to weeks, depending on ambient temperature, with the prolarva gradually transitioning from a lecithotrophic to an exotrophic mode of nutrition as the mouth gapes and retinomotor responses develop.

The maximum reproductive rate of Hymenocephalus italicus has been estimated through comparative scaling relationships grounded in the known reproductive output of Coryphaenoides rupestris. When adjusted for the substantial difference in body mass between these two species, the derived daily rate yields an annual output of roughly 807 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 807 eggs per year] under the stable thermal conditions of the deep Mediterranean. This estimate is evaluated at a habitat temperature of 12.6 °C [T = 12.6 °C], which reflects the prevailing near-bottom water temperature at the depths where mature, gravid individuals have been trawled. The reproductive schedule appears to be limited to a single annual spawning event, suggesting an iteroparous pattern with a possibly synchronous spawning season. Such a strategy is typical of many mid-slope macrourids, whose reproductive cycles are thought to be entrained by seasonal pulses of organic matter flux from the surface.

The adult body mass of Hymenocephalus italicus at its maximum recorded total length is considerable given its small stature, with individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of 47.8 grams [Wwi = 47.8 grams]. This value was obtained from the same length-weight power function used to estimate mass at puberty, calibrated to the specific morphometric relationship for this species. The disparity between the 3.8-gram mass at puberty (3.8 grams) [Wwp = 3.8 grams] and the 47.8-gram asymptotic mass (47.8 grams) [Wwi = 47.8 grams] indicates that a substantial portion of somatic growth occurs after the onset of sexual maturity, a pattern that is common among iteroparous fishes that continue to increase in body size throughout adult life. This post-maturation growth likely contributes to a size-related increase in fecundity, as larger females can accommodate more oocytes and produce larger clutches. The length-weight relationship that underpins these mass estimates was derived from a comprehensive series of individuals spanning the full size range of the species, providing reliable parameterization.

Longevity estimates for Hymenocephalus italicus place the maximum lifespan at approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years], based on the interpretation of annual growth increments in sagittal otoliths from individuals maintained under the stable thermal conditions of their natural habitat at 12.6 °C [T = 12.6 °C]. This lifespan is relatively extended for a fish that matures at just three years of age and achieves a maximum length of only 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters], suggesting a slow pace of life typical of deep-sea species with low metabolic rates. The trade-off between early maturation and prolonged post-reproductive survival indicates that selection may favor repeated spawning over several years rather than a single, high-investment reproductive event. Given a nine-year maximum longevity (9 years) [am = 9 years] and an age at puberty of about three years, the reproductive window spans approximately six years, during which a female could potentially produce multiple annual clutches, each contributing to the overall population recruitment in a resource-limited environment at a temperature of 12.6 °C [T = 12.6 °C].
